moduleB.stem: The graph shows the amount of stable isotope Y in a sample as radioactive isotope X decays to Y. Initially the sample contains 60 units of X and 20 units of Y. After 6 minutes it contains 65 units of Y. What is the half-life of X?
moduleB.tip: Use the increase in Y to find how much X remains.
moduleB.solution: Y has increased by 45 units, so X has fallen from 60 to 15 units. This is one quarter of the original amount, corresponding to two half-lives. Two half-lives take 6 minutes, so one half-life is 3.0 minutes.

distractors.A: Treats the full elapsed time as one half-life.
distractors.B: Uses the final 15 units as though it represented a one-third fraction.
distractors.C: Uses three half-lives instead of two.
distractors.D: Treats four equal fractions as four half-lives.
distractors.F: Doubles the elapsed time rather than dividing it between two half-lives.

moduleB.stem: A slider of mass 0.30 kg is launched up a frictionless slope by a spring compressed 4.0 cm and reaches vertical height h. The same spring is then compressed 6.0 cm to launch a 0.20 kg slider. What maximum vertical height does the second slider reach?
moduleB.tip: Spring energy scales with compression squared, while gravitational energy scales with mass and height.
moduleB.solution: Since 1/2 kx² = mgh, height is proportional to x²/m. The ratio is (6/4)² × (0.30/0.20) = 9/4 × 3/2 = 27/8. The new height is 27h/8.

distractors.A: Uses a linear compression ratio together with the wrong mass factor.
distractors.B: Squares both the compression and mass ratios.
distractors.D: Uses the compression ratio and mass ratio as though both should be squared and multiplied further.
distractors.E: Uses only the inverse mass ratio and ignores the changed compression.
distractors.F: Uses the compression-squared ratio but ignores the lower mass.
